title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
issuing_body: Parliament of India / Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Bill passed by Lok Sabha
Bill passed by Rajya Sabha
Presidential assent; published as Act No. 22 of 2023
Provisions establishing the Data Protection Board (ss. 18-26) and related sections commenced alongside notification of the DPDP Rules, 2025
Remaining substantive obligations scheduled to commence (18 months from Rules notification)

summary: Consent-based statute governing processing of digital personal data by data fiduciaries, with a Data Protection Board as adjudicator. It applies to automated and AI-driven processing because 'processing' is defined to include wholly or partly automated operations.
key_provisions: Processing permitted only on consent (s. 6) or for 'certain legitimate uses' (s. 7); consent notice must state purpose and withdrawal mechanism
Children's data (under 18): verifiable parental consent required; tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children prohibited (s. 9)
Significant Data Fiduciaries (s. 10) must appoint a Data Protection Officer and independent data auditor and conduct periodic Data Protection Impact Assessments
Data principals have rights of access, correction, erasure and grievance redressal (ss. 11-13); no explicit right against solely automated decisions
Penalties up to Rs 250 crore per instance for failure to take reasonable security safeguards (Schedule)
Section 44(3) amends the RTI Act, 2005 to exempt personal information from disclosure
confidence_note: Act text and dates are well established; phased commencement confirmed by MediaNama reporting of the 13 Nov 2025 notification. Exact S.O. numbers for the commencement notifications were not retrieved.

title: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Draft DPDP Rules published for public consultation (comments to 18 Feb 2025, later extended to 5 Mar 2025)
Final Rules notified as G.S.R. 846(E); Rules 1, 2 and 17-21 (Board constitution and functioning) in force immediately
DPDP (Removal of Difficulties) Order, 2026 reportedly issued correcting wording in ss. 9 and 10 of the Act
Rule 4 and First Schedule (Consent Manager registration) in force
Data Protection Board portal dpbi.gov.in opened for Consent Manager applications
Rules 3, 5-16, 22-23 (notice, security safeguards, breach notification, children's data, SDF obligations, rights) scheduled to commence

summary: Subordinate rules operationalising the DPDP Act in three phases over 18 months. They prescribe consent notice formats, breach notification, children's data verification, Consent Manager registration and additional due diligence for Significant Data Fiduciaries including algorithmic software checks.
key_provisions: Three-phase commencement: 13 Nov 2025 (Board), 13 Nov 2026 (Consent Managers, Rule 4), 13 May 2027 (all remaining obligations)
Rule 13: Significant Data Fiduciaries must verify that algorithmic software used for processing 'does not pose a risk' to data principals' rights and must conduct annual DPIA and audit
Rule 10: verifiable parental consent for children's data via reliable identity/age details or virtual tokens; exemptions for health, education and child-care providers listed in Fourth Schedule
Rule 7: personal data breach must be notified to affected data principals without delay and to the Board within 72 hours with details
Rule 4 / First Schedule: Consent Managers must be Indian companies with net worth of at least Rs 2 crore, registered with the Board
Chairperson of Data Protection Board to receive Rs 4.5 lakh per month; Board to function as a digital office
confidence_note: Gazette number G.S.R. 846(E) and phase dates taken from a rule-by-rule tracker citing the gazette and corroborated by MediaNama and India Briefing; the MeitY framework page was not fetched in this session. Some trackers state the Rule 4 date as 14 Nov 2026 (portal launch) rather than 13 Nov 2026.

title: Digital Personal Data Protection (Removal of Difficulties) Order, 2026
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Order S.O. 5458(E) reportedly issued under the Act's removal-of-difficulties power

summary: A removal-of-difficulties order reportedly correcting the wording of section 9(1) and section 10(2)(c)(ii) of the DPDP Act. It is described as a textual fix and not as changing any obligation or commencement date.
key_provisions: Reported S.O. number 5458(E) dated 5 October 2026
Reported to correct wording in s. 9(1) (children's data) and s. 10(2)(c)(ii) (SDF obligations)
Reported not to alter the 13 May 2027 commencement of substantive obligations

title: Data Protection Board of India
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Sections 18-26 of the DPDP Act commenced; Board legally established as a digital office
Government sought nominations for Chairperson and Members
Recruitment advertisement for Chairperson and four Members published in Employment News
Board portal dpbi.gov.in launched for Consent Manager registration

summary: The adjudicatory body under the DPDP Act, empowered to inquire into breaches and impose penalties. As of November 2026 it exists in law and has a portal but no Chairperson or Members have been appointed.
key_provisions: Composition fixed at a Chairperson and four Members under the Rules (Rules 17-21 in force from 13 Nov 2025)
Powers of a civil court for inquiries; may impose penalties up to Rs 250 crore under the Schedule to the Act
Appeals lie to the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT)
No Chairperson or Member appointed as of 1 Nov 2026 despite June 2026 recruitment advertisement
Registration of Consent Managers opened 13-14 Nov 2026 via dpbi.gov.in
confidence_note: Non-appointment status is reported consistently by LiveLaw and two trackers through November 2026; one blog (dpdpguard.ai) claims leadership was appointed, which is contradicted by the others and not corroborated by any official release.

title: Information Technology Act, 2000
issuing_body: Parliament of India / MeitY

timeline.event: Assent; Act No. 21 of 2000
IT (Amendment) Act, 2008 assented, adding ss. 66A-66F, 67A-67B, 69A, 79 safe harbour
Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal struck down s. 66A and read down s. 79(3)(b)
Karnataka High Court in X Corp v Union upheld use of s. 79(3)(b) notices via the Sahyog portal

summary: The principal statute for cyber offences, intermediary liability and government blocking powers. It is technology-neutral and is the legal basis for the 2021 Intermediary Rules and the 2026 synthetic-media amendments; the Government's stated position is that it already applies to AI systems.
key_provisions: s. 66C identity theft and s. 66D cheating by personation using a computer resource (up to 3 years and Rs 1 lakh fine) used against deepfake impersonation
s. 66E violation of privacy (capturing/publishing private-area images), s. 67/67A/67B obscene, sexually explicit and child sexual abuse material
s. 69A blocking of public access to information, with the 2009 Blocking Rules
s. 79 safe harbour for intermediaries conditional on due diligence; s. 79(3)(b) loss of immunity on failure to act on 'actual knowledge' via government or court notice
s. 87 rule-making power used for the IT Rules 2021 and the 2026 SGI amendments
confidence_note: Statute well known; the 27th Standing Committee report (Mar 2026) records MeitY's position that the IT Act is technology-neutral and applies to AI.

title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Rules notified, superseding the 2011 Intermediary Guidelines
Amendment creating Grievance Appellate Committees and requiring intermediaries to 'ensure' user compliance
Amendment adding Fact Check Unit provision and online gaming rules
Amendment tightening who may issue s. 79(3)(b) takedown notices (per Standing Committee record)
Synthetically generated information amendment notified (G.S.R. 120(E)), in force 20 Feb 2026
Draft Second Amendment Rules, 2026 released for consultation

summary: Due-diligence rules that intermediaries must follow to retain safe harbour under s. 79 of the IT Act, plus a code of ethics for digital news publishers and OTT platforms. All deepfake and AI-content obligations on platforms have been inserted into these Rules by amendment.
key_provisions: Rule 3(1)(b): intermediaries must inform users not to host listed unlawful content categories and make reasonable efforts to prevent it
Rule 3(2)(b): removal within 24 hours (reduced to 2 hours in 2026) of non-consensual intimate or morphed imagery on complaint

Rule 4: additional obligations for Significant Social Media Intermediaries (50 lakh registered users), including Chief Compliance Officer, nodal contact, resident grievance officer, monthly compliance reports and first-originator traceability for messaging services
Part III: Code of Ethics and three-tier grievance mechanism for digital news publishers and OTT curated content
Rule 7: non-compliance removes the s. 79(1) exemption
confidence_note: Amendment dates (28 Oct 2022, 6 Apr 2023, 22 Oct 2025) are recorded in the 27th Standing Committee report. The MeitY PDF listed as source_url appears to be the consolidated Rules as amended in 2026 but returned HTTP 403 when fetched.

title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2023
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Amendment notified: Fact Check Unit (FCU) clause in Rule 3(1)(b)(v) and online gaming framework
FCU notified via PIB; Supreme Court stayed the notification the next day
Bombay High Court (tie-breaker opinion of Justice A.S. Chandurkar) struck down the FCU clause as ultra vires Arts 14, 19(1)(a), 19(1)(g) and s. 79 (Kunal Kamra v Union of India)
Supreme Court issued notice on the Union's appeal but declined to stay the Bombay HC judgment

summary: Amendment that would have required intermediaries to remove content about the Central Government identified as 'fake or misleading' by a government Fact Check Unit, and that introduced self-regulatory bodies for online real-money gaming. The FCU clause was struck down by the Bombay High Court and the Union's appeal is pending in the Supreme Court.
key_provisions: Rule 3(1)(b)(v) extended to information 'in respect of any business of the Central Government' flagged by a notified Fact Check Unit
Online gaming: self-regulatory bodies to verify 'permissible online real money games'; KYC obligations for gaming intermediaries
FCU clause held unconstitutional by Bombay HC on 20 Sep 2024; FCU never operationalised
Supreme Court appeal (Union v Kunal Kamra) pending; notice issued March 2026, no stay
confidence_note: Gazette text not fetched; dates from Supreme Court Observer, IFF and news. Exact March 2026 date of SC notice not confirmed (month precision for that milestone).

title: MeitY Advisory to Intermediaries on Deepfakes and Misinformation (26 December 2023)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: MeitY advisory after the Rashmika Mandanna deepfake, reminding platforms of Rule 3(2)(b) 24-hour takedown
Advisory requiring platforms to communicate prohibited content categories clearly and to act on deepfakes under Rule 3(1)(b); 7 days given for action-taken report
Substantive deepfake obligations placed in the Rules themselves by the 2026 amendment

summary: An executive advisory under the IT Rules 2021 directing intermediaries to inform users about the eleven prohibited content categories in Rule 3(1)(b), with specific reference to deepfakes, and to report compliance within a week. It had no independent legal force and was followed by advisories in March 2024 and binding rule changes in 2026.
key_provisions: Platforms to communicate Rule 3(1)(b) prohibitions to users in clear language at registration, login and upload
Users to be informed of penal consequences under IPC and IT Act for deepfake-related offences
Action-taken-cum-status report sought from intermediaries within 7 days
Described by MeitY as a precursor to amending the IT Rules on deepfakes
confidence_note: Advisory text is unpublished on meity.gov.in; content reconstructed from law-firm notes and press. The 7 Nov 2023 precursor advisory date is from recall and press, not a fetched primary.

title: MeitY Advisory on Deployment of AI Models and Deepfakes (1 March 2024, revised 15 March 2024)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Advisory issued requiring 'explicit permission' of Government before deploying under-tested or unreliable AI models to Indian users; action-taken report in 15 days
Minister of State clarified advisory aimed at 'significant platforms', not startups
Revised advisory removed the prior-permission requirement and the 15-day reporting; kept labelling and consent-popup expectations
Labelling/metadata expectations converted into binding Rule 3(3) obligations

summary: A pair of advisories to intermediaries under the IT Rules 2021 on generative AI. The 1 March 2024 version required government permission before deploying under-tested models; after industry objection the 15 March version replaced this with user notification, labelling of unreliability and metadata for AI-generated media.
key_provisions: AI models must not permit users to host or generate unlawful content under Rule 3(1)(b) or threaten electoral integrity
Under-tested/unreliable models to be made available only after labelling 'possible and inherent fallibility' and with consent pop-ups to users
Synthetic audio/visual content that may be used as deepfakes to be labelled or embedded with a permanent unique identifier/metadata identifying the creator or first originator
1 March version's 'explicit permission of the Government of India' requirement withdrawn on 15 March 2024
confidence_note: Advisories were circulated to platforms rather than gazetted; content corroborated by three law-firm summaries and press.

title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2025 (22 October 2025)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Karnataka HC upheld s. 79(3)(b) notices via Sahyog portal, prompting procedural tightening
Amendment notified (date recorded by Standing Committee); reported to take effect 15 Nov 2025

summary: An amendment to Rule 3(1)(d) reported to restrict issuance of s. 79(3)(b) 'actual knowledge' takedown notices to senior officers (Joint Secretary rank or equivalent, DIG rank for police) acting by reasoned written order, with periodic review. The 27th Standing Committee report lists 22 October 2025 as an amendment date of the IT Rules.
key_provisions: Rule 3(1)(d) notices to be issued only by an authorised officer not below Joint Secretary (or DIG for police), by reasoned intimation specifying legal basis and URL (as reported)
Monthly review of notices by a Secretary-level officer (as reported)
Amendment date 22 Oct 2025 confirmed in Standing Committee on Communications and IT 27th Report, para 7
confidence_note: Existence and date confirmed only via the Standing Committee's list of amendment dates; the substantive content (officer rank, reasoned orders, review) is from the researcher's recall and a LiveLaw reference to 'Joint Secretary rank or above' and was not verified against the gazette in this session.

title: Draft IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2025 on Synthetically Generated Information
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Draft amendment and FAQ published for comments
Original comment deadline (reported extension to 13 Nov 2025)
Final amendment notified with changes

summary: Draft rules proposing a definition of 'synthetically generated information' and requiring platforms that create or host it to label it with a visible mark covering at least 10 percent of the visual surface (or the first 10 percent of audio), embed permanent metadata, and obtain user declarations. The 10 percent size rule was dropped in the final version.
key_provisions: Proposed Rule 2(1)(wa) definition of SGI as information artificially or algorithmically created or altered to appear real
Proposed Rule 3(3): label covering at least 10% of visual display or initial 10% of audio duration; permanent metadata/unique identifier; no removal of labels
Proposed Rule 4(1A): SSMIs to obtain user declaration whether uploads are SGI and verify by technical means
Comments invited to 6 Nov 2025; MeitY FAQ published alongside
confidence_note: MeitY FAQ PDF located via search but not opened; the 10% rule and its later removal are reported by iPleaders and by the ECI's parallel adoption of the 10% figure. Comment-deadline extension date is from recall.

title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Draft published for consultation
Notified as G.S.R. 120(E)
Came into force
Gujarat High Court PIL seeks enforcement; intermediaries directed to onboard Sahyog portal
Supreme Court stayed Gujarat HC proceedings pending transfer

summary: India's first binding AI-specific obligations. The amendment defines 'synthetically generated information' (SGI), requires platforms that enable its creation to label it prominently and embed permanent provenance metadata, requires SSMIs to collect user declarations and verify them technically, and cuts takedown timelines to 3 hours for government or court notices and 2 hours for non-consensual intimate imagery.
key_provisions: New Rule 2(1)(wa): SGI is audio, visual or audio-visual information artificially or algorithmically created, generated, modified or altered using a computer resource so as to appear real, authentic or true; text-only output, routine editing, accessibility improvements and document creation are excluded

Rule 3(3): intermediaries offering SGI tools must ensure SGI is prominently labelled and embedded with permanent metadata or a technical provenance mechanism including a unique identifier, and must not permit removal or suppression of labels/metadata; the draft's 10% size requirement was replaced with a qualitative 'prominent' standard

Rule 4(1A): SSMIs must obtain a user declaration on whether content is SGI, deploy appropriate technical measures including automated tools to verify, and display a label on confirmed SGI; 'endeavour to deploy' changed to 'deploy'
Rule 3(1)(d): removal within 3 hours (down from 36) of a court order or reasoned notification from an authorised government officer; Rule 3(1)(b) general categories 36 hours (down from 72)
Rule 3(2)(b): removal within 2 hours (down from 24) of complaints about nudity, sexual acts or impersonation including morphed and deepfake imagery
Grievance resolution shortened from 15 to 7 days; removal of SGI by automated tools deemed not to breach s. 79(2)(a)/(b) conditions; non-compliance forfeits s. 79 safe harbour
confidence_note: Gazette number G.S.R. 120(E), notification date 10 Feb 2026 and commencement 20 Feb 2026 are stated verbatim in the Standing Committee's 27th Report (official text, hosted by MediaNama). Rule-level detail is from Legal500, iPleaders and LiveLaw and is consistent across them. The MeitY PDF returned HTTP 403 and was not read directly. One tracker (indiaairulebook.com) lists a 6 Oct 2026 commencement, which conflicts with the official record and is treated as an error.

title: Draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: Draft released; 15-day comment window to 14 Apr 2026
Comment deadline extended (reports give 29 Apr or 7 May 2026)
No final notification located

summary: A second 2026 draft amendment that would make MeitY advisories, SOPs and codes of practice binding conditions of safe harbour, extend the Part III news code to high-follower individual users ('significant user-publishers of news and current affairs'), and expand Inter-Departmental Committee powers. It remains un-notified as of November 2026.
key_provisions: Proposed Rule 3(4): intermediaries must comply with any clarification, advisory, order, SOP, code of practice or guideline issued by MeitY to retain safe harbour
Proposed new category of significant user-publishers of news and current affairs subject to Part III Code of Ethics, defined by follower threshold
Proposed Rules 3(1)(g)-(h): IT Rules data-retention duties to operate alongside DPDP Act obligations
Proposed Rules 14(2) and 14(5): Inter-Departmental Committee may take up 'matters' referred by MeitY, not only complaints
Comments to itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in; MeitY stated comments would be held in fiduciary capacity and not published
confidence_note: MeitY PDF located but returned HTTP 403; content from SFLC.in, ThePrint and Khaitan. Sources differ on the extended deadline (29 Apr vs 7 May 2026). No gazette notification found through 19 Nov 2026.

title: X Corp v Union of India (Sahyog portal), Karnataka High Court, W.P. No. 7405 of 2025
issuing_body: Karnataka High Court (appeal pending; Supreme Court seized of transfer)

timeline.event: I4C designated as agency under s. 79(3)(b)
MHA launched Sahyog portal for routing takedown notices to intermediaries
Justice M. Nagaprasanna dismissed X Corp's petition in a 351-page judgment
Division Bench (CJ Vibhu Bakhru and Justice C.M. Poonacha) issued notice on X Corp's appeal; listed 11 June 2026
Supreme Court stayed all High Court proceedings on the portal pending the Union's transfer petitions

summary: Single-judge ruling upholding the Government's practice of issuing content-removal notices under s. 79(3)(b) of the IT Act through the Sahyog portal, rejecting X Corp's argument that blocking may occur only under s. 69A with Shreya Singhal safeguards. The portal is the channel through which 3-hour SGI takedown notices under the 2026 Rules are routed.
key_provisions: Held s. 79(3)(b) independently empowers authorised agencies to notify unlawful content; failure to act forfeits safe harbour
Held Shreya Singhal did not confine takedowns to s. 69A, only required a court or government order
Described the Sahyog portal as 'an instrument of public good'; rejected X Corp's standing to assert Art. 19 rights as a foreign company
Appeal pending before Karnataka HC Division Bench; Supreme Court stayed related HC cases on 22 July 2026 while considering transfer
confidence_note: Judgment date, case number and holdings corroborated by LiveLaw, Columbia Global Freedom of Expression and SFLC.in. The 22 July 2026 Supreme Court stay is from a single search summary and should be checked against the SC order.

title: Digital India Act (proposed replacement for the IT Act, 2000)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: MeitY pre-draft consultation presentation (Bengaluru) proposing risk-based regulation of high-risk AI and review of safe harbour
Second consultation (Mumbai); draft promised for mid-2023 but never released
MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan: no standalone AI law planned; DIA described as stalled
Standing Committee 27th Report records MeitY submission that DIA is 'currently under formulation'
Krishnan says MeitY will start stakeholder discussions and 'a process of drafting' on AI regulation
Minister Vaishnaw announces an AI-regulation consultation paper within a month

summary: A long-promised statute to replace the IT Act 2000 with risk-based rules for digital platforms, intermediaries and 'high-risk' AI. No bill or public draft has been introduced in Parliament as of November 2026; the Government has instead amended the IT Rules and signalled a separate AI consultation paper.
key_provisions: 2023 consultation deck proposed regulating 'high-risk AI systems' through algorithmic accountability, risk assessment and vulnerability review
Proposed reconsidering blanket safe harbour for all intermediaries and classifying intermediaries by function
No draft text published since 2023; no bill introduced in Parliament through the Winter Session 2025 or Monsoon Session 2026
MeitY told the Standing Committee in 2026 that DIA is 'under formulation to replace the IT Act and introduce new central legal framework to deal with emerging issues of AI'
confidence_note: Status (no bill, no draft) consistent across MediaNama (Dec 2025, Jul 2026) and the Standing Committee record. The 2023 consultation dates are from recall of MeitY presentations and press, not re-verified this session.

title: MeitY consultation paper on a standalone AI law (announced October 2026)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

timeline.event: MeitY Secretary says no standalone AI law is planned
Minister Vaishnaw says Ministry is discussing a new AI law with industry (month precision)
Secretary Krishnan announces stakeholder consultations and drafting process at CII GCC Summit
Minister Vaishnaw says a consultation paper on AI regulation will be released within a month
No published consultation paper located on meity.gov.in

summary: An announced but, as of 19 November 2026, unpublished MeitY consultation paper intended to found a statute on AI. Ministerial statements say it will cover safety, a 'human-first' approach, skilling, inclusion, deepfakes and psychological harms, with sector-specific guidance for regulators such as banking and securities.
key_provisions: Four stated pillars: safety, human-first approach, skilling, 'no person left behind'
Expected to address deepfakes, psychological harms from AI use and startup compliance burden
Reported design questions: limits on agentic-AI autonomy, consent for synthetic use of likeness or voice, model liability allocation, regulatory sandboxes
Industry reportedly pressing for sector-wise rules and clarity on safe harbour for 'AI intermediaries'; MeitY reported to be weighing a separate 'AI intermediary' definition
Release status unconfirmed as of 1 Nov 2026 per independent tracker and not located by this research as of 19 Nov 2026
confidence_note: Announcement well reported (MediaNama, ThePrint, Outlook Business). Whether the paper was released between 1 and 19 Nov 2026 could not be confirmed because the web-search budget was exhausted; treat as 'announced, not yet published'.

title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (provisions applied to deepfakes and AI-generated content)
issuing_body: Parliament of India / Ministry of Home Affairs

timeline.event: Bharatiya Nyaya (Second) Sanhita Bill passed by Parliament
Presidential assent; Act No. 45 of 2023
Came into force, replacing the Indian Penal Code

summary: The general criminal code. It contains no deepfake-specific offence; prosecutions of AI-generated impersonation, sexual deepfakes and defamatory synthetic media rely on general offences (forgery of electronic records, cheating by personation, defamation, voyeurism, obscenity, criminal intimidation) read with IT Act offences.
key_provisions: s. 336 forgery, including false electronic records (up to 2 years; s. 336(3)-(4) higher terms for forgery to cheat or harm reputation)
s. 319 cheating by personation and s. 318 cheating; s. 351 criminal intimidation
s. 356 defamation (up to 2 years simple imprisonment or fine)
s. 77 voyeurism, s. 78 stalking, s. 79 word/gesture insulting modesty of a woman, s. 294 sale/circulation of obscene material including electronic form
s. 111 organised crime and s. 112 petty organised crime invoked against deepfake fraud networks
No standalone deepfake, synthetic media or AI offence; Rajya Sabha Home Affairs Committee (Aug 2025) and private members' bills seek one
confidence_note: Section numbers for forgery (336) and defamation (356) confirmed by secondary legal commentary; other section mappings (77, 78, 79, 294, 318, 319, 351) are from the researcher's knowledge of the BNS and should be spot-checked against India Code.

title: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (electronic evidence provisions)
issuing_body: Parliament of India / Ministry of Home Affairs

timeline.event: Presidential assent; Act No. 47 of 2023
Came into force, replacing the Indian Evidence Act, 1872

summary: The evidence code. Section 63 governs admissibility of electronic records (including a certificate from the person in charge of the device and an expert), relevant to proving or rebutting AI-generated audio-visual material; it does not itself address authenticity of synthetic content.
key_provisions: s. 61: electronic or digital records are not denied admissibility merely for being electronic
s. 63: conditions for admissibility of electronic records; certificate in the prescribed Schedule form signed by the person in charge and by an expert
s. 39: opinions of experts (including forensic examiners) relevant, used by courts to test alleged deepfakes
Commentators note s. 63 proves a record was produced by a computer resource but not that its content is genuine, leaving a gap for AI-manipulated media
confidence_note: Section numbers 39 and 63 confirmed by two secondary legal sources; statute text not fetched.

title: DPIIT Committee on Generative AI and Copyright: Working Paper Part 1 ('One Nation One License One Payment')
issuing_body: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry

timeline.event: DPIIT constitutes expert committee on AI and copyright (press reports give April or May 2025; month precision)
Working Paper Part 1 released for comments (some reports give 9 Dec)
Original comment deadline
Extended comment deadline closed
Committee last met (per members quoted by Hindustan Times; month precision)
IP academics write to DPIIT asking for publication of a reportedly advanced Copyright Act amendment draft (month precision)

summary: A government committee's proposal for a 'hybrid model' under which all lawfully accessed copyrighted works may be used for AI training under a mandatory blanket licence with statutory remuneration, with no opt-out for rightsholders and royalties collected by a new collective. Part 2 (copyright in AI outputs) has not been published and no Copyright Act amendment has been introduced.
key_provisions: Mandatory blanket licence for AI training on lawfully accessed works; rightsholders cannot withhold works (no opt-out)

Statutory remuneration via a Copyright Royalties Collective for AI Training (CRCAT), a non-profit of CMO representatives; royalties as a flat revenue share payable on commercialisation, set by a government Rate Setting Committee revised every three years
Creators must register works to receive payouts; unregistered works may still be used for training
Rejects both a free TDM exception and pure voluntary licensing; Nasscom dissented in favour of a TDM exception with machine-readable opt-out
Part 2 on copyrightability of AI outputs deferred; committee reported not to have met since June 2026
Reports in July 2026 of a Copyright Act amendment 'at an advanced stage' are unconfirmed; no draft published
confidence_note: Official PDF located on dpiit.gov.in (HTTP 403 on fetch); content consistent across MediaNama, Ikigai Law and SpicyIP. Committee constitution date conflicts (April vs May 2025) and chair/membership were not confirmed. Status of a Copyright Act amendment is unverified (single HT-derived report).

title: Copyright Act, 1957 (as applied to AI training and outputs)
issuing_body: Parliament of India / DPIIT

timeline.event: Copyright (Amendment) Act, 2012 in force (statutory licensing ss. 31C-31D, s. 52 fair dealing expanded)
ANI v OpenAI filed in Delhi HC, first Indian suit on AI training
DPIIT committee proposes amendments for a mandatory licensing regime
Delhi HC holds prima facie that training-stage storage is fair dealing under s. 52(1)(a)(i)

summary: The copyright statute, with no AI-specific provision. Section 52(1)(a)(i) (fair dealing for private or personal use including research) was held prima facie to cover LLM training in ANI v OpenAI; s. 2(d)(vi) treats the person who causes a computer-generated work to be created as its author. Amendment proposals from the DPIIT committee are pending.
key_provisions: s. 2(d)(vi): author of a computer-generated literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work is 'the person who causes the work to be created'
s. 52(1)(a)(i): fair dealing for private or personal use including research; relied on by Delhi HC (interim) for training-stage copying
s. 14 and s. 51: reproduction and storage rights; infringement
ss. 31C-31D statutory licences cited by DPIIT committee as model for an AI-training licence
No amendment introduced in Parliament as of Nov 2026 despite July 2026 reports of a draft
confidence_note: Statutory provisions from standard knowledge of the Act; the copyright.gov.in URL is the standard location of the Act text but was not fetched this session.

title: ANI Media Pvt Ltd v OpenAI OpCo LLC & Anr, Delhi High Court (interim order, 24 July 2026)
issuing_body: Delhi High Court (Justice Amit Bansal)

timeline.event: Suit filed; summons issued; amici curiae appointed (Dr Arul George Scaria and Adv. Adarsh Ramanujan)
Interventions by DNPA, Indian Music Industry, Federation of Indian Publishers (for ANI) and Broadband India Forum, Flux Labs, IGPP (for OpenAI) (month precision)
Judgment reserved after 32 hearings
Interim injunction refused in 135-page judgment; suit continues

summary: The first Indian judicial finding on LLM training. The court refused ANI an interim injunction, holding prima facie that OpenAI's storage of ANI articles for training falls within fair dealing under s. 52(1)(a)(i) of the Copyright Act, that ChatGPT outputs were not substantially similar to ANI's works, that ANI failed to prove memorisation/regurgitation, and that an injunction would harm the public at large. title: TEC Standard 57050:2023 - Fairness Assessment and Rating of Artificial Intelligence Systems
issuing_body: Telecommunication Engineering Centre (TEC), Department of Telecommunications

timeline.event: Standard released (month precision; 2023 edition)
Updated edition reported

summary: A voluntary TEC standard providing a procedure to assess and rate the fairness of AI systems, aimed at telecom and ICT deployments but drafted to be sector-agnostic. It uses a three-step method: bias risk assessment across the AI lifecycle, selection of fairness metrics and thresholds, and quantitative bias testing producing a Bias Index and Fairness Score.
key_provisions: Step 1: survey-based bias risk assessment across seven lifecycle stages on a five-point scale
Step 2: questionnaire to fix system intent, protected attributes, stakeholders and mandatory fairness metrics with threshold values

Step 3: group fairness metrics (statistical parity difference, disparate impact, equal opportunity difference, average odds difference, equalised odds) aggregated into a Bias Index and Fairness Score/rating
Voluntary; cited by MeitY's 2025 AI governance guidelines and the Standing Committee as an available assurance tool
TEC has also issued related work on AI robustness assessment (not verified in this session)

summary: Ruling striking down the 2023 IT Rules clause that would have obliged intermediaries to remove content about Central Government business flagged as fake by a government Fact Check Unit. The court found it vague, chilling of speech and beyond s. 79 of the IT Act. Relevant to AI because it limits the Government's ability to use the IT Rules to designate truth without statutory backing, a constraint on future misinformation and synthetic-media regimes.
key_provisions: Rule 3(1)(b)(v) (as amended 2023) held ultra vires Arts 14, 19(1)(a), 19(1)(g) and s. 79 IT Act
'Fake, false or misleading' held vague; Government cannot be arbiter of truth about itself
FCU never operationalised; Union appeal pending in Supreme Court with notice issued March 2026
